raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old male with a history of illicit drug use (cocaine and marijuana), and no significant medical history, was initially hospitalized for dengue fever with warning signs, confirmed by Non-Structural Protein 1 (NS1) antigen testing. Treatment included hydration therapy and antipyretics. Four days after discharge, the patient developed dyspnoea on moderate exertion, orthopnoea, and bradycardia, prompting readmission. Subsequently, he was referred to our institution for evaluation and management of severe bradycardia.
On admission, heart rate was 41 b.p.m., blood pressure 137/63 mmHg, and respiratory rate 13 breaths/min. Physical examination revealed bradycardic heart sounds, with otherwise unremarkable findings. Blood pressure remained stable throughout the episodes of third-degree atrioventricular (AV) block, with systolic pressures ranging between 110 and 130 mmHg and diastolic pressures between 70 and 80 mmHg, all within normal limits. Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation with a low ventricular response, along with T-wave abnormalities in Leads II, III, and aVF (Figure 1A). Metabolic studies during hospitalization were normal. Additional findings included Troponin-I at 24.3 pg/mL (reference range <17 pg/mL), Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB) at 4.3 ng/mL (reference range 0-6.3 ng/mL), and B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) at 63 pg/mL (reference range 0-100 pg/mL). The initial transthoracic echocardiogram revealed mild left atrial dilation with a volume index of 37 mL/m2 and preserved biventricular systolic function, including a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) of 24 mm. The left atrial strain was measured at 16% (Figure 2). Transoesophageal echocardiography did not detect thrombi in the left atrial appendage. Two electrical cardioversions were attempted at 200 J each, resulting in temporary atrial pacing with nodal escape rhythm (Figure 1B).
Holter monitoring revealed first-degree atrioventricular block with a PR interval of 400 ms, second-degree Mobitz 2 atrioventricular block, third-degree atrioventricular block, four sinus pauses, the longest being 3.8 s, and migratory atrial rhythm (Figure 3). Antiarrhythmic therapy was not considered during episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation due to the presence of bradycardia and atrioventricular block. Anticoagulation was also not initiated because the CHA2DS2-VA score was 0 points, and there was no evidence of thrombi on echocardiography. The patient underwent an exercise stress test using the Bruce protocol to assess chronotropic response, revealing sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, and nodal rhythm, with a maximum heart rate of 160 b.p.m. (during atrial fibrillation) and achieving 10.2 METS (metabolic equivalents) with functional Class I (Figure 4). Coronary computed tomography angiography showed no evidence of atherosclerotic disease, normal coronary artery origins with left dominance, a calcium score of 0 AU, and CAD-RADS of 0.
The patient was hospitalized for 7 days. Conservative management was chosen because the patient remained asymptomatic and showed no signs of circulatory compromise, leading to gradual recovery observed over a 30-day follow-up. The discharge criterion was based on a good chronotropic response during the exercise stress test. Holter monitoring at 30 days revealed only first-degree atrioventricular block with a minimum heart rate of 39 b.p.m., and at 6 months, the patient presented with sinus rhythm and a resting heart rate of 58 b.p.m. on ECG (Figure 5).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old male presented with exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, and severe bradycardia 4 days after hospital discharge for dengue fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was initially hospitalized for dengue fever with warning signs and treated with hydration and antipyretics. Four days after discharge, he developed dyspnea on moderate exertion, orthopnea, and bradycardia, leading to readmission and tertiary referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of illicit drug use (cocaine and marijuana); recent hospitalization for dengue fever with warning signs; no other significant medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea on moderate exertion and orthopnea; remained asymptomatic without syncope or circulatory compromise during subsequent inpatient bradyarrhythmia episodes.

objective.physical_examination: Heart rate 41 bpm, blood pressure 137/63 mmHg (remaining stable at 110-130/70-80 mmHg during complete AV block episodes), respiratory rate 13 breaths/min, and bradycardic heart sounds with otherwise unremarkable physical exam.
objective.routine_investigations: Normal metabolic studies; Troponin-I 24.3 pg/mL (reference <17 pg/mL), CK-MB 4.3 ng/mL (reference 0-6.3 ng/mL), and BNP 63 pg/mL (reference 0-100 pg/mL). ECG showed atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response and inferior T-wave abnormalities (leads II, III, aVF); two 200 J electrical cardioversions yielded temporary atrial pacing with nodal escape rhythm. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed mild left atrial dilation (37 mL/m2), LVEF 65%, TAPSE 24 mm, and left atrial strain 16%; transesophageal echocardiography excluded left atrial appendage thrombi. Holter monitor demonstrated first-degree AV block (PR 400 ms), Mobitz type II second-degree AV block, third-degree AV block, four sinus pauses (longest 3.8 s), and migratory atrial rhythm. Exercise stress test (Bruce protocol) achieved 10.2 METs (functional Class I) and a maximum heart rate of 160 bpm.
objective.advanced_workup: Coronary CT angiography showed normal coronary artery origins with left dominance, no atherosclerotic disease, calcium score 0 AU, and CAD-RADS 0.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Post-dengue myocarditis/conduction system dysfunction presenting with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and transient high-grade/third-degree atrioventricular block, confirmed by prior positive dengue NS1 antigen test, mildly elevated Troponin-I (24.3 pg/mL), and normal coronary CT angiography. Managed conservatively without permanent pacing, antiarrhythmics, or anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VA score 0) over a 7-day hospitalization given preserved chronotropic competence on exercise testing. At 30-day Holter follow-up only first-degree AV block (minimum HR 39 bpm) persisted, and at 6 months ECG showed normal sinus rhythm at 58 bpm.
